description: This Congressional Research Service report explains how the US Emergency Alert System is built on a structure conceived in the 1950s, when over-the-air broadcasting was the best way to warn the public widely. FEMA and the FCC jointly administer EAS with the National Weather Service; NOAA weather radio has an all-hazard warning capability, and the report covers the Digital Emergency Alert System, the Integrated Public Alert and Warning System (IPAWS), the WARN Act of 2006 that funded public television stations to install alert equipment, and the Commercial Mobile Alert System planned for April 2012. It discusses shifting goals that delayed IPAWS and the challenges ahead: standards, user acceptance, system management and funding. There are 20 editions from August 2004 to December 2010, so the report also records how the system's plans changed. Producer: Congressional Research Service; site run by the University of North Texas Libraries. Coverage: United States. Access: free HTML, PDF and EPUB; the summary and edition list were read, the full text was not. Licence and cost: free; no licence statement read. Caveats: content is dated to 2010, before later IPAWS and WEA rules, and describes plans, not measured performance. Simulation uses: the description of alert chains and responsibilities supports emergency-response models of broadcast-based warning. Related record: the US nationwide alert test of 2023 (case_study-us-nationwide-alert-test-2023).
